title: New crash handler in macOS?
body: I wrote a test app with an intentional crash scenario and saw an unfamiliar crash-handler experience. This is not a problem report so much as two questions: is this new, and are the runtime maintainers aware of it? I attached a screenshot of what appeared.

symptoms_visible: When my test app intentionally crashes, an unfamiliar crash-handler interface appears.
N0.label: N0 unfamiliar crash handler reported

symptoms_visible: A one-line unhandled managed exception invokes the Swift crash backtrace interface.
Starting the same command with SWIFT_BACKTRACE set to enable=no prevents that extra interface from appearing.
N1.label: N1 Swift handler and startup toggle reproduced

symptoms_visible: The Swift crash interface still appears when I try to disable it programmatically from my managed application.
N2_x.label: N2_x managed-code workaround aftermath

symptoms_visible: The same Swift crash interface appears with .NET 10 on macOS 15.6, while my C and Ruby crash tests do not show it.
Official .NET 8 and .NET 9 builds do not show the interface in the corresponding test on macOS 26.
N2.label: N2 issue shown not to be macOS 26 only

symptoms_visible: The downloaded Preview 6 SDK does not show the Swift interface, but a locally built runtime from the same Preview 6 tag does.
A locally built runtime from the v9.0.7 tag also shows the Swift interface, even though the downloaded .NET 9 build did not.
N3.label: N3 official and local build behavior compared

symptoms_visible: The interface appears with dotnet run, but not when I invoke the built DLL directly with dotnet.
Piping dotnet run so that it does not have the usual terminal connection also prevents the interface from appearing.
A cross-built runtime still shows the same crash interface.
N4.label: N4 startup environment and TTY conditions isolated

symptoms_visible: I have not retested a build containing the host mitigation, so I cannot personally confirm that the extra Swift crash interface no longer appears.
N_terminal.label: N_terminal mitigation shipped without reporter retest

question_patterns: What text or runtime name appears in the unfamiliar crash output?
Can you paste the identifying text from the crash interface?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The extra crash output identifies itself as the Swift backtrace or Swift debugger interface.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: There is no Swift text at all; this is the standard macOS crash reporter for a native access violation.

question_patterns: Which .NET and macOS builds reproduce this, and can you reduce it to a minimal unhandled exception?
Does a one-line throw reproduce the same interface?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I can reproduce it with .NET 10 Preview 7 and macOS 26 Preview 7 using a one-line program: throw new Exception("hello!");. I was not using a debug runtime build.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It only happens in my large application with a custom native crash library; a one-line throw exits normally without the extra interface.
The same one-line throw reproduces on the next macOS beta build as well.

question_patterns: If you start the process with SWIFT_BACKTRACE set to enable=no, what happens?
Can you run the same repro with SWIFT_BACKTRACE="enable=no" and report whether the extra crash interface still appears?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Running SWIFT_BACKTRACE="enable=no" dotnet run disables the Swift backtrace interface for the same crashing program.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The Swift interface still appears with SWIFT_BACKTRACE="enable=no" set before dotnet starts.

edges.comment: From c3-c5. The reporter supplied the beta context and crash-test gist; participant1 supplied the minimal reproduction and environment-variable probe. Both affected operators are folded into one simulated user side.

solution.intent: Disable the Swift backtrace handler from managed application code after the process has started.
solution.concrete_example: At the beginning of Main, set SWIFT_BACKTRACE to enable=no before executing the code that may throw.

edges.comment: From c7: participant1 attempted to disable the behavior programmatically from the application and found that doing so after managed startup was ineffective.

question_patterns: Do equivalent crashes in plain C or another language show the same interface?
Can you compare this with a C abort and a Ruby SIGABRT on the same machine?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A plain C program calling abort() and Ruby calling Process.kill('ABRT', Process.pid) terminate with SIGABRT but do not invoke the Swift backtrace interface. A C null dereference does not invoke it either.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: C, Ruby, and .NET all display the identical extra crash interface on this machine.

question_patterns: Can this be reproduced on a non-beta macOS release?
Please try the same minimal throw on macOS 15 and tell me what appears.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. I reproduced the same Swift crash interface with .NET 10 on non-beta macOS 15.6.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It only reproduces on macOS 26 beta; the same runtime and program have ordinary exception output on macOS 15.6.
It also reproduces on another stable macOS 15 point release.

question_patterns: Do downloaded .NET 8 or .NET 9 builds show this on the same macOS 26 machine?
Can you run the same throw using official .NET 8 and .NET 9 installations?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I cannot reproduce the extra Swift interface with official .NET 8 or .NET 9 builds on macOS 26 beta.

edges.comment: From c10 and c13-c14. Participant1 ran the C, Ruby, stable-macOS, and earlier-.NET comparisons; the affected contributors are folded into the simulated user side. These observations falsified the early macOS-26-only theory.

question_patterns: Which downloaded .NET 10 preview first shows the behavior?
Can you compare the official Preview 6 and Preview 7 SDKs with the same program?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The downloaded .NET 10 Preview 6 SDK does not end in the Swift debugger, while the downloaded Preview 7 SDK does.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every downloaded preview I tested, including Preview 5 and Preview 6, shows the same Swift interface.

question_patterns: Do local builds from the Preview 6 and .NET 9 tags behave like their downloaded official builds?
Can you build an older runtime tag locally and run the same throw?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: A local Debug build from the Preview 6 tag shows the Swift debugger even though the downloaded Preview 6 SDK does not. I also built the v9.0.7 tag locally, and that local .NET 9 runtime still reproduces the Swift interface.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Local and downloaded builds match exactly: neither Preview 6 nor .NET 9 shows the interface.
A different local Debug configuration gives the same local-versus-official split.

question_patterns: Are the entitlements on the official Preview 6 and Preview 7 dotnet executables different?
Can you compare the signing entitlements of the two downloaded preview hosts?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I compared the entitlements of the official Preview 6 and Preview 7 builds, and they were identical.

question_patterns: Do you have output showing the framework description and the crash behavior from the local older build?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes. My attached output prints the local runtime's framework description and then shows the Swift backtrace after the deliberate exception.

edges.comment: From c16 and c18-c23. Participant5 compared official and local Preview 6 builds and entitlements; participant1 built v9.0.7 locally and attached the screenshot. The evidence made a source-commit bisection unreliable and walked back the claim that this was simply a .NET 10 code regression.

question_patterns: Does the behavior differ between dotnet run and directly invoking the built DLL with dotnet?
Please compare dotnet run with dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/app.dll.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I can reproduce it with dotnet run, but not when I invoke the built app directly as dotnet bin/Debug/net10.0/app.dll.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both invocation forms always show the identical Swift interface.

question_patterns: What happens if dotnet run is piped so its output is not attached to the normal terminal?
Can you compare an interactive terminal run with a piped run?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The extra Swift interface does not appear when I run the command through a pipe, for example dotnet run | echo.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The Swift interface appears even when standard output is piped and there is no interactive terminal.

question_patterns: What code-signing status flags do you get for the official and locally built dotnet hosts?
Can you compare the CSOps output for a host that shows the handler and one that does not?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: For the official Preview 7 host that stopped showing the handler, CSOps included CS_HARD, CS_KILL, and CS_RUNTIME. My local runtime host lacked CS_HARD and CS_RUNTIME. Forcing the feature on in the official host printed that backtrace-on-crash is not supported for privileged executables.

question_patterns: Can you test a runtime and host cross-built on x64 to rule out the arm64 build pool?
Does switching the build to an x64 Mac change the crash behavior?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I used a cross-built runtime and host, and it still showed the same crash interface.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The x64 cross-built host does not show the interface while the arm64-built host consistently does.

edges.comment: From c26-c28 and c37-c42. Participant5 supplied raw CSOps results, participant6 compared invocation modes and TTY behavior, and participant7 tested the x64 cross-build. These contributors are folded into one simulated user side.

solution.intent: Mitigate the intentionally activated Swift crash backtrace in the native .NET host by setting SWIFT_BACKTRACE=enable=no before the Swift runtime's static initialization, while preserving an explicit user setting.
solution.concrete_example: In the native host, before loading code that initializes the Swift runtime, set SWIFT_BACKTRACE to enable=no only when the variable is currently unset. Apple confirmed that the handler behavior was intentional and that the setting is read during process startup. A mitigation using this approach was subsequently reported as shipped for .NET 10.
solution.inference_hint: The thread never fully isolates why particular official and local builds differ. The accepted conclusion is narrower: Apple confirmed intentional Swift backtrace-handler activation; the handler is sensitive to startup context such as TTY and privileged/hardened status; and SWIFT_BACKTRACE must be set by the native host before Swift static initialization. Do not present an unproven .NET source commit, macOS 26 alone, or a specific signing flag as the definitive root cause.

edges.comment: From c44-c50. Apple advised either an early dummy signal handler or SWIFT_BACKTRACE=enable=no and emphasized that the environment variable is checked at process startup. Maintainers selected the host-level environment-variable mitigation and later reported .NET 10 behavior restored to the .NET 9 baseline. No affected reporter posted a retest after that mitigation shipped.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted diagnosis at the level established by the thread: the extra crash interface is the Swift runtime backtrace handler, whose activation was confirmed by Apple as intentional and whose behavior depends on process-startup context; it is not exclusively a macOS 26 crash reporter or a proven .NET source-code regression.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: SWIFT_BACKTRACE=enable=no suppresses the interface when present at startup, stable macOS also reproduces it, official and local builds differ, and terminal attachment changes the behavior.
The mitigation must run in the native host before Swift runtime static initialization, setting SWIFT_BACKTRACE=enable=no when the user has not already supplied an explicit value.
Must not recommend setting SWIFT_BACKTRACE from managed Main as the fix, because that in-case attempt occurred after the Swift initializer and did not suppress the handler.
Must not claim that an x64 cross-build fixes the problem or that macOS 26 alone caused it; both directions were contradicted by the collected tests.
Must ask an affected user to retest a build containing the host-startup mitigation and must not declare the reporter's system resolved without that verification.

persona_hint.experience_level: Highly technical .NET contributor who can create minimal crash repros, test preview and nightly SDKs, compare runtime versions, discuss signing and CI behavior, and coordinate deeper runtime investigation.
persona_hint.communication_style: Brief and direct, often framing observations as FYIs or questions; raises release-risk concerns, shares repro code, and invites focused experiments from other runtime specialists.
